## Answer: none of the conversion is taxable for 2025 ($0 taxable income)

Daniel moved $7,000 into his traditional IRA (SYN-15870003) on 11 Feb 2025 and converted all $7,000 to his Roth IRA (SYN-15870004) on 14 Feb 2025. Under the pro-rata rule, the share of a conversion that is tax-free equals his after-tax money (basis) divided by the total in all his traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs. On Form 8606:

- **After-tax money:** $0 carried in from 2024, plus the $7,000 nondeductible 2025 contribution, gives $7,000.
- **IRA balance at year end:** the IRA held $0 on 31 Dec 2025. It had no holdings and no cash. The $7,000 converted was added back in, so the total is $7,000.
- **Ratio:** $7,000 ÷ $7,000 = 1.000, so the whole $7,000 is tax-free.
- **Result:** **$0 taxable (line 18)**, and **$0 after-tax money carried to 2026 (line 14)**.

Three points behind this:
- **The 401(k) doesn't count.** His former employer's 401(k) (SYN-15870002, $178,338.60 at year end) is an employer plan, not an IRA, so it stays out of the calculation. Leaving pre-tax money there was the plan agreed in December 2024.
- **The contribution couldn't have been deducted anyway.** Their 2025 joint wages were $377,000, above every income limit for deducting IRA contributions. That makes the $7,000 genuinely after-tax.
- **The 1099-R overstates the taxable amount.** It shows box 2a as $7,000 with box 2b ("taxable amount not determined") checked. The return has to include Form 8606, or the full $7,000 will look taxable.

**Unconfirmed:** our records only cover accounts at this firm. The $0 result holds only if Daniel had no other traditional, SEP or SIMPLE IRA anywhere else on 31 Dec 2025. Nothing on file suggests one, but he needs to confirm it.
